text: Hey folks, Dan Mlelen here. We have all
grappled from time to time with that
age-old question, should I call this
person a Pharisee? But now, thanks to
the good folks over at Erdman's, we have
this edited volume, Judeophobia and the
New Testament texts and context, which
includes literally dozens of essays on
Judeophobia and the New Testament. And
for a limited time only, they've thrown
in this handy dandy Pharisees flowchart,
which will help you grapple with that
question. Let's walk slowly through this
very complex process. We start with the
question, should I call this person a
Pharisee? Well, step number one, did the
person live in or before the first
century CE? If the answer is no, don't
call them a Pharisee. If the answer is
yes, we move on to step two. Was the
person actually a Pharisee? Again, if
the answer is no, don't call them a
Pharisee. If the answer is yes, then we
move on to the final and the most
complex stage of this process. Are you
using the word as an insult? If the
answer is yes, don't call them a
Pharisee. If the answer is no, then it's
probably safe. Folks, the porative use
of the term Pharisee as a way to refer
to someone as an overly legalistic
religious person is not only
historically inaccurate, it's just plain
old anti-semitic. The good folks over at
Erdman's are providing you for a limited
time only this handy dandy Pharisees
flowchart. Feel free to refer back to it
anytime you are struggling with the
question of whether or not you should
call a person a Pharisee. I'm Dan
Mlelen. Thank you for your time. And the
fit for this video has been Powerman.
